item.title: Keys
item.description:
A key is a named permission for exactly one action, such as Create Organization, Approve Catalog Request, or Download Token. Every authorization decision in Layer5 Cloud comes down to one question: does this user hold the key this action requires, in this organization? Understanding keys tells you why a user can or cannot do something, and whether the model fits the access rules you need.

How a key reaches a user 🔗

Keys roll up in three layers. A keychain groups related keys, a role groups keychains, and a user holds roles in an organization or a team. A user never receives a key directly: granting a key means placing it in a keychain that belongs to a role the user holds.

item.title: Keychains
item.description:
A keychain is a named bundle of keys. It sits between the single permission and the role a person holds:

  • A key allows one action, such as Create Token.
  • A keychain groups related keys, such as everything needed to manage teams.
  • A role groups keychains, and users hold roles in an organization or team.

A user’s effective keys in an organization are the union of the keys in every keychain of every role the user holds there. A keychain grants nothing by itself. It takes effect only through a role that includes it.

item.title: Sessions
item.description:
A session is the credential Layer5 Cloud issues each time someone signs in. It is what keeps a browser tab, a second device, or a connected Meshery Server signed in, and it is what you end when you want one of those sign-ins to stop working. Sessions expire on their own; API tokens do not.

One session per sign-in 🔗

Every sign-in creates its own session. Each browser, device, and Meshery Server that signs in through Layer5 Cloud holds a separate session with its own expiry, and any number of them can be active at once. Ending one session leaves the others untouched.

item.title: Tokens
item.description:
An API token lets software act as you. Scripts, CI/CD pipelines, mesheryctl and other Meshery clients present it to Layer5 Cloud instead of signing in through a browser. Because a token carries your full authority and never expires, deciding how many tokens to create, who holds them and when to delete them is a security decision. This page explains how tokens behave so you can make it.

What a token is 🔗

A token is a credential bound to your user account. A client sends it as a bearer token in the Authorization header of each request; the Cloud API reference shows the exact form.
